subject: Vocabulary
description: Word pairs commonly tested with subtle distinctions in meaning

questions.explanation: GENEROUS = giving freely, willing to share. ANTONYM = STINGY / MEAN / MISERLY / TIGHT-FISTED / PARSIMONIOUS / NIGGARDLY (latter has fallen out of use due to phonetic confusion). Distractors are similar-LOOKING words but different meaning: GENTEEL (refined), GENERIC (typical/non-branded), GENUINE (real). DEEP INSIGHT — 'false friends' in vocab: words that LOOK similar but mean very different things — common SSC trap. EXAMPLES: principle vs principal; affect vs effect; complement vs compliment; stationary vs stationery; lose vs loose. Always read CAREFULLY.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.explanation: CONCEAL = hide, keep secret. ANTONYM = REVEAL / DISCLOSE / EXPOSE / DIVULGE / UNCOVER. Roots: con- (with/together) + celare (to hide) → 'hide together / fully'. Same root: ceiling (covers); cellar (hidden room). Other CON- words with hidden meaning: CONFISCATE (seize), CONFINE (restrict), CONCEDE (give up). PRACTICAL: in diplomacy + journalism + science — CONCEAL evidence is often illegal; REVEAL of state secrets = espionage. INSIGHT — Latin/Greek prefixes change meaning radically: ad- (toward), de- (away from), in- (in or not), pre- (before), post- (after), un- (not), re- (again), trans- (across).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.explanation: TRANSPARENT (clear, see-through; figuratively HONEST + open). ANTONYM = OPAQUE (blocks light; figuratively HIDDEN, hard to understand). TRANSLUCENT (in between — frosted glass, allows partial light). FIGURATIVE: 'transparent governance' (openness, accountability); 'opaque dealings' (hidden, suspicious). RTI ACT (2005, India) → key transparency tool. RECENT: digital transparency (open data, govt portals, blockchain). KEY DISTINCTION: TRANSPARENT = total visibility; TRANSLUCENT = partial; OPAQUE = none. WORD ROOTS: 'trans-' (across) + 'parens' (appearing) → 'appearing through'. OPAQUE from L. opacus = shaded. ASSOCIATED WORDS: lucid (clear), murky (unclear), lucent (shining), opacity (n).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.explanation: AMATEUR = does an activity for love (Latin AMARE = to love); not paid; often unskilled. ANTONYM = PROFESSIONAL = paid expert; high level. SUBTLE distinction: amateur ≠ unskilled (some amateurs are very good); just NOT PAID. Opposite of UNSKILLED = SKILLED. PYQ TRAP: students mix amateur + beginner. NOTE — in OLYMPICS earlier, only AMATEURS could compete (until 1980s; this changed in 1990s allowing professionals). IPL = professional cricket; clubs in cities = amateur. INSIGHT: word origin reveals positive original meaning ('lover of') — degraded over time to 'unskilled'. Same trend with: 'silly' (originally 'happy/blessed'), 'awful' (originally 'awe-inspiring').
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.explanation: OPTIMIST (Latin optimus = best) — sees BEST in everything; positive outlook. ANTONYM = PESSIMIST (Latin pessimus = worst) — sees WORST. REALIST sees things AS THEY ARE — middle ground. CYNIC distrusts motives. PRAGMATIST seeks practical solution. INSIGHT — these aren't fully opposed; psychology shows OPTIMISM benefits health, longevity, social bonds (Martin Seligman's 'Learned Optimism'); but excess optimism = naive (DUNNING-KRUGER, irrational exuberance). PESSIMISM has 'defensive' value — preparing for worst case. BALANCE: REALISTIC OPTIMISM = ideal — hope + plan + adapt. Famous quotes: 'Pessimist sees difficulty in every opportunity; optimist sees opportunity in every difficulty' (Churchill).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.explanation: ASCEND (Latin ad- + scandere = to climb) = go UP. DESCEND = go DOWN. Same root: SCALE (climb, ladder); STAIR (related); ESCALATE (go up rapidly). FIGURATIVE: 'ascend to throne' (become king); 'descend into chaos' (deteriorate). DON'T CONFUSE: ASSENT (agree — 'gave assent') vs ASCENT (act of going up — 'mountain ascent'). HOMOPHONES! Many common confusions: hear/here, weak/week, dear/deer, principal/principle, complement/compliment. Vocabulary discipline = recognise root + spelling pairs. ASCERTAIN = find out (different word entirely; 'ascert' from L. certus = certain; ad- + certus → make certain).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.explanation: ACQUIT (legal: declare NOT GUILTY in court) ↔ CONVICT (declare GUILTY). Both refer to court verdicts. INSIGHT: legal vocabulary worth knowing — PLEA, BAIL, REMAND, ARRAIGN, INDICTMENT, SUBPOENA, AFFIDAVIT, INJUNCTION, PERJURY, EXTRADITE, PARDON, CONFESSION. INDIAN COURTS: Magistrate < Sessions Court < High Court < Supreme Court. JUDGE issues a JUDGEMENT; LAWYERS argue; jury (in some countries — India HAS NO JURY since 1959 KM Nanavati case; verdicts go directly to judge). DOUBLE JEOPARDY (Article 20(2)) — can't be tried twice for same offence (once acquitted, can't be tried again — unless special circumstances).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Which of the following is most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to 'SERENE'?
questions.explanation: SERENE means calm, peaceful, and untroubled. Its antonym is TURBULENT — wildly agitated and disturbed. Options A, C, and D are all synonyms or paraphrases of SERENE itself. Candidates who rush often pick D ('pleasantly still'), which reinforces rather than contradicts the word.

questions.stem: Select the option that is most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to 'FRUGAL'.
questions.explanation: FRUGAL means economical and careful with money, avoiding waste. Its antonym is EXTRAVAGANT — spending lavishly without restraint. Options B, C, and D are all synonyms of FRUGAL. The distractor in D ('wisely avoiding expenditure') is a close restatement of the word's own dictionary definition.

questions.stem: Which option gives the meaning most OPPOSITE to 'BENIGN'?

options.option_text: gentle and essentially harmless in nature
friendly and wholly unlikely to cause harm

questions.explanation: BENIGN means gentle, harmless, or not threatening — used both generally and medically (benign tumour). Its antonym is MALIGNANT — aggressively harmful and destructive. Options A, B, and D are all near-synonyms of BENIGN. Candidates often confuse 'benign' with 'boring' and miss the hostile/medical angle entirely.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to 'ALLEVIATE'?

options.option_text: ease the burden of a difficult state
intensify and further worsen a condition

questions.explanation: ALLEVIATE means to make pain, suffering, or a problem less severe. Its antonym is AGGRAVATE or EXACERBATE — to intensify and make worse. Options A, B, and C are all restatements of the meaning of ALLEVIATE. The trap is that all three wrong options sound subtly different, tempting candidates to overthink.

questions.stem: Choose the word or phrase most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to 'LUCID'.

options.option_text: clearly expressed and very easy to follow
hopelessly muddled and hard to interpret

questions.explanation: LUCID means clear, coherent and easily understood (of writing or speech), or mentally alert (of a person). Its antonym is OBSCURE or MUDDLED — confused and difficult to interpret. Options A, C, and D reinforce the meaning of LUCID. Candidates drawn to D confuse the medical sense ('lucid intervals') with a separate concept of sharpness.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to 'SANGUINE'?

options.option_text: buoyantly hopeful and confident in outcomes
cheerfully positive and full of expectation

questions.explanation: SANGUINE (from Latin 'sanguis' — blood, linked to a rosy complexion denoting good cheer) means optimistic especially in a difficult situation. Its antonym is DESPONDENT or PESSIMISTIC — gloomy and disheartened. Options A, B, and D are all restatements of the meaning of SANGUINE. Many candidates confuse SANGUINE with 'composed' and choose vague distractors, missing the specifically optimistic core.

questions.stem: Select the option that is most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to 'LACONIC'.

options.option_text: excessively wordy and long-winded in speech
deliberately choosing to use very few words
restrained and markedly sparing with words

questions.explanation: LACONIC (from the Spartans of Laconia, renowned for extreme brevity) means using very few words; concise to the point of seeming curt. Its antonym is VERBOSE or GARRULOUS — using far too many words. Options B, C, and D are all definitions of LACONIC itself. The classical allusion makes this difficult; even candidates who know the root often fail to identify VERBOSE as its precise antonym.
